overview.today_plain: Horizon is Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 rewritten from scratch in Rust, so it runs faster on the same computer. MineComplex's servers, resource packs and server plugins work today, started from the MineComplex launcher.
overview.today_dev: A native Rust and wgpu reimplementation of Java 26.3: the same saves, rules and terrain, checked against the real game by more than 300 differential harnesses (a Java oracle and a Rust probe on the same inputs). Two programs: `horizon-client` only joins servers, and worlds run on `horizon-server` behind the proxy.
overview.help_plain: Play it and tell us what differs from vanilla (Discord or GitHub), run the benchmark on your computer, vote for what you want next, or pick one of the Help wanted items.
overview.help_dev: Read CONTRIBUTING.md, pick a Help wanted item or a To do card, check vanilla's code for the behaviour, and paste the block `python3 tools/pr_ready.py` prints in your pull request.

items.title: Steady frames at long render distances
items.plain: Making Horizon faster than vanilla on every computer, with smooth camera movement even at 32 chunks, by spreading the work better over the processor's cores.
items.dev: Frame pacing at render distance 32 (#678): long frames come from work competing with the render thread. In review: world generation workers build free structure starts instead of queueing them (#1760), the worker pool leaves one core as vanilla does (#1778), and the terrain vertex arena is read as storage where flat draws run (#1742). Still open: CPU-bound fields of block entities (#717). Every change shows before and after numbers from `tools/perf_bench.py` against vanilla 26.3 (docs/benchmark.md).

items.title: Faster block lookups
items.plain: Speeding up the code that reads and writes the blocks of the world, which almost everything in the game goes through: generation, lighting, meshing and ticking.
items.dev: `PalettedContainer` and `PackedStorage` find an entry's word by multiply and shift instead of an integer division (#1790, #1794); meshing looks up baked models by index, not by name (#1747). Each change keeps the paletted storage harnesses identical and shows its microbenchmark (docs/performance/paletted-container-access-results.md).

items.title: Playing on servers: everything shows as it should
items.plain: When you play on a server, other players, mobs, items and menus look and behave as in vanilla: skins, poses, item names, inventories and server networks.
items.dev: Client-of-a-server fixes in `game/remote*.rs` and `horizon-protocol`: mobs' aggressive and item-use flags (#1802, #1798), ghost items after a remote menu (#1795), skins (#1652), cookies and transfer packets for proxy networks (#1650), firework boosts (#1671), living-entity attributes and simulation distance (#1731), styled item names (#1702), primed TNT between updates (#1710).

items.title: Server dialogs and login screens
items.plain: Servers that show dialogs, such as the register and login screens of AuthMe, will work in Horizon.
items.dev: 26.3's dialog packets and model (#1720), the dialog screen with its buttons and actions (#1734), then text and boolean inputs (#1735).

items.title: Play in your language
items.plain: Item names, container titles and server messages follow the language you pick, as in vanilla. Today parts of the game stay in English.
items.dev: Translatable components resolved through the selected language for items, containers and server text (#1806), on top of the bundled languages the prepared resources carry (#1594). Left: the client's own screens (#1672) and the main menu with zh_cn (#1774).

items.title: Shader packs, written again from scratch
items.plain: Shader packs were removed and are being rebuilt from scratch. They come back, off by default, once the best-known packs draw properly.
items.dev: A clean-room rewrite in `horizon-shaderpack`, from the packs' public format documentation only: reading packs, the preprocessor and `.properties` files are merged (#1584, #1585, #1586); translating programs to WGSL through naga, buffers, uniforms and the terrain, entity, sky, weather and hand stages are in review (#1698 to #1801).

items.title: Discord Rich Presence
items.plain: Your Discord profile can show that you are playing Horizon, with a switch to turn it off.
items.dev: A Discord IPC client on its own thread (#1787) and the presence with its setting (#1788). Merged: it ships with the next release.

items.title: A leaner codebase that builds faster
items.plain: Cleaning up Horizon's code: removing what nothing uses and making it quicker to build, so fixes and new features land faster.
items.dev: A review of the whole tree: dead code and stubs removed (#1432, #1658), one probe binary per crate (#1453, #1454), shared harness helpers (#1448), clippy clean on the whole tree (#1707). docs/architecture.md maps each feature to its files and harnesses.

items.title: Horizon's own shader format and kit
items.plain: Horizon's own way to make shader packs, with tools to write and test them. Every pack is checked before it runs, and the registry will list them.
items.dev: `horizon-shader-api` (API 0.1, experimental): WGSL stages with typed inputs inside the renderer's passes, options as WGSL override constants, and the `horizon-shader new|check|pack` tool with templates and the example pack Golden Hour. Merged: the check every pack passes (#1820) and the tool, templates and guide (#1822). In review: the post stage running in the game with hot reload (#1861), the sky stage (#1863) and registry checks that use the game's own check (#1855). Left: the material, lighting and shadow stages, a last-good fallback on reload, a GPU-time overlay per stage and budgets (docs/shaders.md, docs/api/shaders.md). The Iris/OptiFine loader is a separate item, 'Shader packs, written again from scratch'.

items.title: Pre-generate an area with /pregen
items.plain: A /pregen command that builds an area of the world ahead of time, so players don't wait for new terrain when they explore.
items.dev: Generates, lights and saves an area before anyone walks there (#1805, a contributor's pull request, in review). Useful on servers, and it moves the generation cost away from the first visit; the generation speed-ups are under 'Steady frames at long render distances'.

items.title: Fresh benchmarks against vanilla
items.plain: New public numbers comparing Horizon with vanilla on many kinds of computers, measured the same way every time, with a history that shows what each release changed.
items.dev: Redo the comparison after the current performance work (#1073); reliability, coverage and presentation (#1346); a scene must count as loaded only once its first chunk arrives (#1749). Next: a performance history across releases (an automatic comparison of each release with the last, on a timeline), more report fields (server TPS and MSPT, power, battery drain, temperature, throttling) and more hardware (a MacBook on battery, low-end laptops, community reports). Reports come from `horizon-client --benchmark` (docs/benchmark.md).

items.title: Pistons push players and mobs
items.plain: Pistons and slime blocks will push players, mobs and items as in vanilla. Today moving blocks pass through them.
items.dev: Port `PistonMovingBlockEntity.moveCollidedEntities` and `moveStuckEntities` (honey), the slime bounce and `Entity.limitPistonMovement` for `MoverType.PISTON`, for a server's players. Issues #1496, #1609, #1608, #1704, #1758.

items.title: Horizon on Intel Macs
items.plain: Builds of the game for Macs with an Intel processor.
items.dev: x86_64 game builds, picked per processor (#1171). Before it ships it needs a run on a real Intel Mac: Rosetta on Apple Silicon only proves the CPU code. Requests: #1161, #1792.

items.title: Faster world creation and entry on small CPUs
items.plain: Creating a world and joining it should be quick even on a four-thread laptop, where a fresh world at 32 chunks can make you wait minutes for the first terrain.
items.dev: Cut the per-column generation cost (noise sampling, surface rules, aquifers) and the lock convoy on structure starts, and leave one core free for the rest of the game as vanilla does (#1760 and #1778, in review, are listed under 'Steady frames at long render distances'). Still to profile on small CPUs: the first seconds of a fresh world deliver no chunk, and fluids remesh for about a minute after loading. Measured with `tools/perf_bench.py` (docs/benchmark.md, docs/profiling.md).

items.title: Servers that hold 20 TPS with 50 to 100 players
items.plain: Servers that keep 20 ticks per second with 50 to 100 players. Today Horizon holds it up to 50 bots and drops to about 10 at 100.
items.dev: Measured against vanilla on equal work (docs/server.md, Scale): Horizon is ahead with few players and when exploring, but vanilla's tick is shorter with 25 to 50 players near spawn. Ideas on the list: send entity changes instead of rebuilding every entity each tick (about 15 percent), fewer memory reads in random ticks and collision scans, cheaper item collision checks, mob AI and natural spawning. The bot benchmark (`horizon-bots`) is the proof.

items.title: Low-end computers: Steam Deck, old Macs, 8 GB
items.plain: Horizon should run well on small machines: integrated graphics, the Steam Deck, older Macs and 8 GB of memory, with a battery mode that saves power on laptops.
items.dev: Partly done: an opt-in 60 FPS cap with fewer workers on battery and animated textures on the GPU (both shipped). Left: measured targets and fixes per class of machine (memory use, worker counts, startup) on a Steam Deck, old Intel and Apple Silicon Macs and 8 GB computers, reported in docs/benchmark.md.

items.title: Native upscaling
items.plain: Draw the game at a lower resolution and sharpen it to your screen's size, in the way of FSR or DLSS, to gain frames on weaker graphics cards. An optional graphics setting.
items.dev: A render-scale setting below the window size with an upscaler of our own that runs on every wgpu backend. Proof: frame time against native resolution on integrated GPUs, and screenshots for image quality. Issue #1403.

items.title: A batch of targeted optimisations
items.plain: Several smaller speed-ups, each measured: idle block entities that sleep, cheaper particles, faster structure placement, high-rate mice and very large texture packs.
items.dev: Block entities and hoppers that skip work when idle (the hopper item scan is already skipped when no item is near); a particle frustum test first (also a parity gap), then particle quads built on the GPU; jigsaw shortcuts that skip blocked connectors and pool elements known not to fit, with layouts unchanged (trial chambers and ancient cities first); batched raw mouse input on Windows for 8000 Hz mice; a better atlas packer for huge resource packs (a 64x pack builds a 704 MiB atlas for 452 MiB of textures); sign-heavy scenes (#1461). Profile first, keep what pays, show before and after numbers.

items.title: Prepare a version without Java
items.plain: Set up Horizon, a server first, without Java on your computer: published tables are combined with your own copy of the game.
items.dev: Today `horizon-prepare` runs Mojang's exporters with Java. Issue #1750 proposes publishing the computed version tables once from CI and assembling the rest locally from the player's own jar and assets, provided the tables hold no Mojang content; a contributor offered a pull request, and it would help phones too. A server-only prepare from `server.jar` alone is the first step (docs/server.md).

items.title: Server console, bans and a full admin API
items.plain: Manage a server from a console, ban and pardon players, and drive it from other tools through a full admin API and an MCP server for AI agents.
items.dev: `horizon-server console` (a text interface), `ban`, `pardon`, `ban-ip` and `mcp` over stdio. Admin API additions: the player list, kick, ban, op and whitelist, an SSE stream of logs and events, a text metrics endpoint, config GET and PATCH, backup delete and download. The panel's later features (bans, worlds, server.properties import, logs and crash reports) and vanilla's management protocol (the JSON-RPC over WebSocket that the `management-server-*` keys configure), so vanilla's tools can manage a Horizon server. docs/server.md, docs/api/server.md.

items.title: An official Docker image for servers
items.plain: An official image to run a Horizon dedicated server in Docker with one command, your own copy of the game files mounted in.
items.dev: The repository has the Dockerfile (`packaging/server/Dockerfile`: a multi-stage build on Debian bookworm-slim, user `horizon`, volume `/data`, port 25565, game files mounted read-only, `HORIZON_EULA` and friends answering the first-start questions), and anyone can build it (docs/hosting.md, section 9). Left: publish the image to a public registry from the release workflow, tagged per release, so it follows the same checks, and update the docs. The image never holds Mojang's files.

items.title: Villages and combat, exactly as in vanilla
items.plain: Villages and fights behaving as in vanilla: iron golems defending villages, villagers remembering their homes, mace smashes and knockback.
items.dev: Villages: iron golem village goals, villager memories across saves, villager age, job-site claiming on dedicated servers, flower offers (#1639 is one report). Combat: the mobs' `attack_knockback` attribute, mace smash logic, the hit knockback source on the host, the fire burnout biome tag. Each is checked against vanilla by a harness (docs/rust-parity.md).

items.title: Choose the audio output device
items.plain: Pick the speakers or headphones Horizon plays through, in Music & Sounds.
items.dev: An output device list in Music & Sounds, falling back to the system default. #1035 started it: a player on an older Windows computer had no sound at all, and a device choice is how such cases are found and fixed.

items.title: Well-known shader looks, rewritten for Horizon
items.plain: Popular shader packs rewritten in Horizon's format, so good packs exist from the start. Only packs whose licence is open source and compatible with ours are rewritten, never anything else.
items.dev: The first candidates are Photon, Chocapic13 and MakeUp Ultra Fast, each only after its licence is read and recorded: a pack is rewritten only if it is open source and compatible with Horizon's licence, and the rewrite is written from the shader format's documentation and the look on screen, not from anyone's code. Today only the Golden Hour example exists (`crates/horizon-shader-api/packs/golden_hour`).

items.title: Wayland and Hyprland polish
items.plain: Fixes for Linux desktops that use Wayland and Hyprland: fullscreen, the clipboard, the GUI scale after a restart and the like.
items.dev: Open: the GUI Scale is clamped to 2 after a restart under Hyprland, while XWayland keeps it (#1866). Earlier reports covered fullscreen dropping on menu clicks, the clipboard and a white overlay (#1007, closed). Checked on a real Wayland session.

items.title: A versioned agent-control protocol
items.plain: A stable, documented way for AI agents and scripts to drive the game, with versions and an event stream so tools keep working as Horizon changes.
items.dev: `hello` answers with the API version, the release and the features; `horizon-ctl --api`; MCP serverInfo; reply schemas generated into the reference; a `test.` namespace for hooks; transcript compatibility tests; `subscribe` as a stream of events on one connection; Horizon option files by key and saved-server commands. Agent control itself (`horizon-ctl`, both MCP servers, the No AI switch) is done: docs/agent-control.md, docs/api/agent-control.md.

items.title: Pipeline protection and a GitHub App for agents
items.plain: Safer releases: changes to the release machinery need the owner's review, and AI agents use a smaller identity of their own instead of a personal account.
items.dev: `.github/CODEOWNERS` lists the workflows, the release and signing tools, the update-checking code and the installers (#1015); the branch protection that makes it count waits for the `horizon-agent` GitHub App, which reads and writes code, pull requests and issues but can't change settings, workflows, secrets or members, and whose tokens last an hour. It needs the owner to create the App and switch the protection on (docs/security.md).

items.title: An optional AI teammate
items.plain: An optional AI teammate you can talk to by voice. It plays beside you, helps or finishes the game with you, runs on your computer first, and exists only if you turn it on. The No AI switch hides it.
items.dev: Draft pull requests: the companion (#1068), its safety modes and their evaluation (#1069) and a route that finishes the game (#1070). In the drafts: a companion that follows, fights, mines, crafts, sleeps and respawns; chat and push-to-talk voice, with speech recognition and a choice of voices; presets (very strong, helper, beat the game); a guard model with Clean, Kid and Salty modes; perception levels from Fair to All-knowing; hardware detection with a simple mode and an Advanced tab; local models first, cloud keys optional. The No AI switch is already in the game. Left: the speedrun route doesn't finish the game reliably yet, voices for more languages, and the safety evaluation, which must pass before it ships.

items.title: Every Minecraft version, prepared automatically
items.plain: Every past and future Minecraft version prepared for Horizon automatically. When Mojang releases one, Horizon follows it, and every system is checked against it again.
items.dev: The port pipeline (docs/version-ports.md, `tools/version_port.py`) detects a release, prepares it, diffs its classes against the pinned 26.3, regenerates the data-driven tables, runs every parity harness on it and writes a port report that becomes issues. The goal is as little human work as possible for any version, past or future. Detection and the first slices are merged; the scheduled agent that runs it every day isn't installed yet. Two versions in one build are out of scope.

items.title: A light default shader pack
items.plain: A small built-in look (tone mapping, colour grade, a cheap vignette) that costs almost nothing, for players who want a nicer picture without a heavy pack.
items.dev: An opt-in, composite-only pack on the native shader API, under about 0.3 ms at 1080p, shown on the Shader Packs page. Pack option sliders and profiles, and a Failed row with the full error, belong with it.

items.title: Optional ray tracing
items.plain: An optional ray-tracing mode for graphics cards that support it (RTX and recent AMD): shadows, water reflections and global lighting on top of the vanilla look.
items.dev: A spike with ray-traced sun shadows, off by default, is a draft (#1180). Reflections, global illumination, Apple M3 and newer if it is cheap, and a performance report per card come after.

items.title: HDR monitors
items.plain: Output for HDR monitors: brighter highlights and richer colour where your screen supports it.
items.dev: Issue #1441. Needs a surface format and a tone-mapping path per backend, and tests on real HDR screens on Windows, macOS and Linux.

items.title: MSAA, anisotropic filtering, exclusive fullscreen
items.plain: More graphics options: multisample anti-aliasing, anisotropic filtering and an exclusive fullscreen mode. Today Horizon has FXAA and borderless fullscreen.
items.dev: Not implemented (docs/graphics.md). Anisotropic filtering needs linear magnification in wgpu, which blurs close blocks, so close-up sharpness has to be kept first; MSAA would sit beside FXAA; exclusive fullscreen where the backend supports it.

items.title: A complete video studio inside the game
items.plain: Record, replay and edit videos without leaving the game: record in a keypress, replay a session, cut and finish the video. One of Horizon's original goals.
items.dev: Three stages. Recording: capture gameplay in a keypress with an encoder thread and little frame-time cost. Replay: a replay mode for recorded sessions. Editing: cuts, camera paths, titles and export. None of it exists yet; the agent-control socket (docs/agent-control.md) already lets tools drive the game for scripted shots.

items.title: Controllers: tested on real pads
items.plain: Make controller support solid: tested with real PlayStation and Xbox pads and a Steam Deck.
items.dev: The game side is merged (docs/controllers.md): pads read with gilrs, menus, rumble, glyphs, remapping and DualSense adaptive triggers, lightbar and haptics, but not yet confirmed on real pads or a Steam Deck (DualSense haptics stay behind a switch until then). Left: a test pass on real hardware.

items.title: The full debug screen
items.plain: Vanilla's complete F3 screen: debug options, a profiler chart, ten-second captures and an atlas dump.
items.dev: Today F3 shows position, chunk, light, biome and FPS (docs/native-client.md). Vanilla also has F3+F6 debug options with profiles, F3+1 the profiler pie, F3+L a ten-second capture and F3+S the atlas dump (#562 asked for the F3 editor).

items.title: Horizon on Linux ARM64
items.plain: Game builds for 64-bit ARM Linux computers.
items.dev: Issue #1709: aarch64 builds of the game in the release workflow, tested on a real ARM machine with its Vulkan driver. The server build already drops audio and controllers (`--no-default-features`).

items.title: OpenGL for old computers
items.plain: Horizon now starts on old PCs whose graphics card has no Vulkan or DirectX 12 driver: it switches to OpenGL by itself, and Options > Graphics can pick OpenGL by hand.
items.dev: wgpu's GL backend (WGL on Windows, EGL on Linux) as the last fallback after Vulkan and DirectX 12 (#1917), sprite arrays and CPU sprite animation for drivers without compute (#1920), no indirect draws below GL 4.3 (#1936). Minimum OpenGL 3.3 core. Shader packs don't run on it yet.

items.title: Android, iOS and the browser
items.plain: Versions of Horizon for Android, iOS and web browsers. Nothing official yet; contributors have started the first pieces.
items.dev: No official build. Android was first closed as not planned, with touch controls, a mobile interface, packaging and loading the player's own assets all missing; the roadmap now includes it, iOS and a WebAssembly build for the browser as long-term goals. First pieces from contributors: `horizon-dualsense` compiling on iOS (#1813) and helper-thread limits on Android (#1751). Preparing without Java (#1750) matters here too. Horizon ships none of Mojang's files on any platform.

items.title: Benchmark your computer
items.plain: Run Horizon's built-in benchmark and share the report: every new computer makes the performance work more accurate. No coding needed.
items.dev: `horizon-client --benchmark standard` writes a JSON report (docs/benchmark.md); attach it to an issue. Example: #1711.

items.title: End city banners keep their pattern
items.plain: Banners in End cities show as plain magenta instead of with their pattern.
items.dev: Compare the banner block entities the End city templates place with vanilla's (`EndCityPieces`, the templates' block entity NBT, `BannerBlockEntity`'s patterns), in `crates/horizon-world/src/worldgen/structure/`. Issue #1438; possibly related: #526.

items.title: Enchanted loot in End cities
items.plain: Armour and tools in End city chests should come enchanted, as in vanilla.
items.dev: `loot.rs` implements `enchant_with_levels`: find why the End city chest table's rolls come out bare, and compare them with vanilla's for a few seeds. Issues #1437, #1660.

items.title: Cooldowns drawn on items
items.plain: After you throw an ender pearl, its slot should show the cooldown sweeping away, as in vanilla.
items.dev: Vanilla draws `ItemCooldowns`' percent as a white overlay over the slot (`GuiGraphicsExtractor.itemDecorations` and `itemCooldown`) in the hotbar and in inventories. Issue #1763.

items.title: Chat settings and team prefixes
items.plain: The Hidden and Commands Only chat settings should hide chat, and team prefixes should appear before names in chat.
items.dev: Vanilla checks `ChatVisiblity` before it delivers chat and system messages (#1376), and chat uses the team-formatted display name (#1378). Both issues have exact steps to reproduce.

items.title: A pointing hand over buttons
items.plain: The mouse pointer should turn into a pointing hand over menu buttons, as in vanilla 26.3.
items.dev: 26.3's `AbstractWidget` asks for a cursor from `CursorTypes` when it is hovered; winit's `CursorIcon::Pointer` gives the same shape. Issue #1347.

items.title: Ctrl+Backspace and scroll bars in menus
items.plain: Ctrl+Backspace should delete a whole word in the creative search, and every list's scroll bar should be draggable.
items.dev: `EditBox` deletes by word with Ctrl (#1764); the Game Rules and Statistics lists' scroll bars can't be dragged (#1782, after #978).

items.title: Chickens flap while they fall
items.plain: Chickens should flap their wings while they fall, not stand still in the air.
items.dev: Vanilla's `Chicken.aiStep` updates `flap` and `flapSpeed` when the chicken isn't on the ground, and the model's wings follow them. Issue #1706.

items.title: Server resource packs
items.plain: Servers can send you their resource pack: Horizon asks, downloads it and applies it, like vanilla.
items.dev: The dedicated server offers server.properties' pack (#1562); the client's pack manager, downloads, prompt and Server Resource Packs setting (#1569, #1570).

items.title: GPU occlusion culling on Macs
items.plain: On Macs the GPU now skips terrain hidden behind hills and caves: 8 to 48% more frames per second at 32 chunks on an M4 Pro.
items.dev: GPU occlusion culling on Metal (#1434).

items.title: Animated textures on the GPU
items.plain: Water, lava and other animated blocks are now animated by the graphics card: 1.7 to 2.4 times better 1% lows on Intel graphics.
items.dev: Frames uploaded once, no per-tick CPU blend or copy (#1239).

items.title: Dynamic lights
items.plain: An optional extra: torches you hold, drop or set on fire light up what is around them.
items.dev: Held, dropped and burning light sources (#1162), in Horizon Extras, off by default.

journal.title: Single player becomes a server, servers send their packs
journal.plain: Single player now runs on its own server thread, as vanilla does, and a run of fixes made shields, tridents, elytra, maps, fishing, signs and books work there and for every server player. Servers can send you their resource packs, the launcher got its blocky new look, and the first pieces of Horizon's mod registry landed. Shader packs were taken out, to come back written from scratch.
journal.dev: The server thread became the default (#1514), after guests and server-thread players reached parity: totems (#1463), death drops (#1464), signs and books (#1465, #1466), shields, tridents, crossbows and spyglasses (#1476), elytra (#1475), maps (#1510), fishing (#1509), wind charges (#1508), strikes and mob effects (#1512), the cursor stack on close (#1513). Server resource packs: the dedicated server offers them (#1562) and the client downloads, asks and applies them (#1569, #1570). Mod registry: index schema 1 and `.hpack` (#1634), `cargo horizon-mod check` (#1642), the submission service (#1659). Shader packs were removed (#1561) and the clean-room rewrite started from the format's documentation (#1584 onward). Releases now ship in batches of five pull requests, or six hours after the oldest (#1554).
